title: Signature Requirements for Clinical Notes: Timeliness, Late Entries and Attestations
summary: What makes a signature valid under CMS rules, when an attestation or signature log fixes a gap, how late entries work, state and payer signing deadlines, co-signatures for pre-licensed clinicians, and an unsigned-note control that keeps audits clean.
body_markdown:
Medicare's signature requirements say a clinical note must identify the clinician who provided the service, by handwritten or electronic signature, and show when the service happened. Medicare sets no universal signing deadline; it expects documentation at the time of service and accepts an attestation from the author for most missing signatures, though not on orders that require one. States and payers often set hard deadlines, such as three business days for most Medi-Cal behavioral health notes in California.


This guide covers what makes a signature valid under the CMS Program Integrity Manual, how attestations, signature logs and late entries work, state and payer deadlines, treatment plan and co-signature rules, e-signature controls, and what an unsigned note costs in an audit. For the clinical content a signature vouches for, see our[medical necessity documentation guide](https://blog.adentris.com/medical-necessity-documentation-behavioral-health/) . It is general information, not legal advice.


The short version


- A valid Medicare signature identifies the author: handwritten or electronic, and legible or backed by a signature log. Rubber stamps are out unless the author has a documented physical disability.
- Medicare has no fixed signing deadline. States and payers do: three business days for most Medi-Cal behavioral health notes, seven days for SUD service documentation in Minnesota, and before the claim goes out under some commercial policies.
- The author can fix a missing signature with an attestation, except on orders that require one and on anything that had to be signed by a set date.
- Late entries are fine if they carry their real date and author. Backdating is not.
- Run a daily unsigned-note report and hold the claim until the note is signed. Some Medicaid and commercial reviewers deny unsigned notes outright.


## What counts as a valid signature under Medicare


The rules sit in the Medicare Program Integrity Manual (PIM), Chapter 3, §3.3.2.4 (current text effective January 17, 2025). It says signatures matter for two reasons: to meet a specific signature requirement in a statute, regulation, national coverage determination (NCD) or local coverage determination (LCD), and to settle doubts about whether a record is authentic.


That framing shapes how reviewers treat a missing signature. If a rule requires the signature and an attestation doesn't resolve the gap, the contractor may deny the claim. If no rule requires it, the reviewer asks whether the signature is needed to identify the author. If it isn't, the reviewer disregards the gap and reviews the rest of the record. If the record raises authenticity concerns, the reviewer can pursue an attestation, a denial or a fraud referral.


Signature method Medicare position What to watch


**Handwritten** Accepted. A mark or sign showing knowledge, approval, acceptance or obligation Illegible initials need a signature log or attestation


**Electronic** Accepted The system must be protected against modification, and the signer and provider answer for its authenticity


**Rubber stamp** Not typically accepted Allowed under the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 only for an author with a physical disability who can prove it


**Scribe or AI-drafted note** The scribe need not sign The treating clinician must sign. CMS applies the same rule to AI transcription


**Undated signature** Accepted if the date can be determined Reviewers may infer the date from dated entries above and below it


The AI line deserves attention. Per the July 2025 MLN fact sheet, if you use a scribe, "including artificial intelligence technology," you sign the entry to authenticate it, and you don't need to record who or what transcribed it. An AI-drafted note is still the clinician's note, and the signature means the clinician read it.


## Signature logs and attestation statements


A signature log is a typed list of clinicians' names next to their handwritten signatures or initials. Reviewers must consider every log regardless of when it was created, and they can't deny a claim because the log lacks credentials, though CMS encourages listing them. A log fixes legibility. It can't supply a signature that was never made.


An attestation can. To count, it must be signed and dated by the author of the entry and identify the patient. When a contractor needs one, it asks whether you want to send an attestation or log within 20 calendar days of the phone call or the letter, and the review clock extends by 15 days once it arrives. CERT reviews are exempt from both timeframes.


Situation Attestation accepted? Source


Progress note the author forgot to sign Yes, from the author, whenever it was created PIM §3.3.2.4(D)


Illegible signature on a note or plan Yes, or use a signature log PIM §3.3.2.4(C) and (D)


Order that requires a signature No MLN905364, July 2025


Plan of care that had to be signed before treatment began Only to identify an illegible signature, never to backdate PIM §3.3.2.4(D)


Attestation signed by a colleague, even in the same group No PIM §3.3.2.4(D)


Attestation with no underlying record entry No PIM §3.3.2.4(D)


CMS doesn't require a format, but it publishes sample language you can use as is:


Signature attestation statement (CMS sample language, PIM §3.3.2.4)


Patient: \[Name\] | Date of birth or Medicare ID: \[Identifier\] | Record entry: \[Note type\] for date of service \[Date\]


"I, \[print full name of the physician/practitioner\], hereby attest that the medical record entry for \[date of service\] accurately reflects signatures/notations that I made in my capacity as \[insert provider credentials, e.g., M.D.\] when I treated/diagnosed the above listed Medicare beneficiary. I do hereby attest that this information is true, accurate and complete to the best of my knowledge and I understand that any falsification, omission, or concealment of material fact may subject me to administrative, civil, or criminal liability."


Signature: ____________________ | Date signed: \[Today's date, never the date of service\]


Treat attestations as a repair tool, not a workflow. The author has to be reachable and willing to sign under that liability language, which gets harder when a clinician has left the program. And a stack of attestations in one ADR response tells the reviewer something about your signing habits.


## Late entries, amendments and corrections


PIM §3.3.2.5 starts from one expectation: services are documented in the record at the time they are rendered. When something has to be added or fixed later, the date and author of the amendment, correction or delayed entry must be identifiable, and the change must be "clearly and permanently" marked. Reviewers then apply the same signature rules to it. If they find potentially fraudulent entries, they refer the case to the UPIC.


Payers write similar rules. Centene's Marketplace behavioral health documentation policy (revised April 2026) requires each addendum to reference the original note and carry its own completion date, name, signature and credentials. It also says addenda clarify or correct a note and should not substantively change the nature, length or content of the service.


A compliant late entry looks like this: "Late entry, written 11/06/2026 at 9:12 a.m. by \[name, credentials\], for the individual session on 11/04/2026. Client reported..." The original note stays untouched, and the EHR audit trail shows both timestamps. A backdated note, created today but dated to look as if it was written on the day of service, is a different act. In an audit it reads as falsification, and no attestation fixes it.


## How fast notes must be signed


Medicare's payment rules don't set a number of days. Hospital conditions of participation come closest: entries dated, timed and authenticated, and the record completed within 30 days after discharge (42 CFR 482.24). Psychiatric hospitals follow their own record rules instead (42 CFR 482.61). The PIM reminds reviewers that conditions of participation aren't conditions of payment, but surveyors check them. Elsewhere, the hard deadlines come from states, accreditors and payers.


Source Rule Applies to


**California, DHCS BHIN 23-068** Progress notes within 3 business days of the service, including any required co-signatures. Crisis notes within 1 calendar day Medi-Cal specialty mental health and Drug Medi-Cal services


**Minnesota, Minn. Stat. 245G.06** Each treatment service documented within 7 days. Every entry signed and dated, with the staff member's title Licensed SUD treatment programs


**Minnesota, Minn. Stat. 245I.08** Treatment supervisor approval within 10 business days for assessments and treatment plans written by trainees and practitioners Licensed mental health services


**Medicare, 42 CFR 482.24 and 482.61** General hospitals: entries authenticated, record complete within 30 days after discharge. Psychiatric hospitals: psychiatric evaluation within 60 hours of admission, progress notes at least weekly for the first two months Medicare-certified hospitals


**The Joint Commission, RC.01.03.01** A written policy requiring timely entry into the record Accredited behavioral health organizations


**Centene Marketplace policy** Entries signed with credentials before the claim is submitted Behavioral health claims to its Marketplace plans


The Joint Commission row matters more than it looks. The standard doesn't pick a number. It makes you pick one, and a survey can then hold you to it. Set it no looser than the strictest state or payer rule you bill under. If you have California Medi-Cal patients, three business days is your number.


## Treatment plan and certification signatures


Treatment plans carry more signatures than progress notes, and some of them have dates attached by regulation. That makes them the place where an attestation is least likely to save you.


- **Medicare PHP.** The plan is established and periodically reviewed by a physician, with the diagnosis, the type, amount, duration and frequency of services, and the goals. Recertification must be signed by a physician who treats the patient, first as of the 18th day of services and then at least every 30 days (42 CFR 424.24(e)).
- **Medicare IOP.** The same plan elements, with physician recertification at least every 60 days (42 CFR 424.24(d)). Our[IOP and PHP billing guide](https://blog.adentris.com/iop-php-billing-documentation-guide/) covers the rest of the certification content.
- **Patient signature, Minnesota SUD programs.** The individual treatment plan must be signed by the client and the alcohol and drug counselor within 10 days of starting residential services, and within 14 days in opioid treatment programs. Changes need both signatures too. For telehealth, the counselor can document why a signature isn't possible and record verbal or electronic approval.


Missing signatures on assessments and plans show up in federal audits. In a 2026 audit of Maine Medicaid autism services, HHS-OIG estimated at least $45.6 million in improper payments, and its findings included assessments missing the signatures of the staff who did them or of parents or guardians.


## Co-signatures for pre-licensed clinicians and interns


Co-signature rules depend on who pays, and they don't always do what programs assume. A co-signature shows supervision. It doesn't turn an ineligible rendering provider into an eligible one.


- **Medicare incident-to.** Behavioral health services by auxiliary personnel can be furnished under general supervision, and the supervising practitioner doesn't have to be the one treating the patient more broadly. Only the supervising practitioner may bill (42 CFR 410.26(b)(5)). The person who provided the service still signs their own note, since no one may sign or attest for another author.
- **California Medi-Cal.** Required co-signatures fall inside the same three-business-day window as the note, per Los Angeles County's guidance on BHIN 23-068.
- **Minnesota.** Assessments and treatment plans completed by a clinical trainee or behavioral health practitioner need documented treatment supervisor approval within 10 business days.
- **Commercial.** Centene's Marketplace policy requires the rendering provider to be independently licensed and lists provisionally licensed psychologists, licensed master social workers and licensed associate counselors among those who don't qualify. A supervisor's co-signature doesn't change that.


## E-signature system controls


CMS's guidance on electronic signatures is short: systems need protection against modification, administrative safeguards should meet recognized standards and laws, and both the signer and the provider are responsible for authenticity. The HIPAA Security Rule fills in the technical floor.


Control Why it matters in an audit Source


Unique login for every user, no shared accounts A signature from a shared login can't identify its author 45 CFR 164.312(a)(2)(i)


Audit trail of creation, signing and every edit Shows a late entry was labeled, not backdated 45 CFR 164.312(b)


Signed notes locked, changes only by addendum Meets the "clearly and permanently" standard for amendments 45 CFR 164.312(c)(1), PIM §3.3.2.5


Identity verification at sign-in Ties the signature to a verified person 45 CFR 164.312(d)


No signing on another clinician's behalf Reviewers reject attestations from anyone but the author PIM §3.3.2.4(D)


Watch batch signing. EHRs that let a clinician sign 40 notes with one click produce valid signatures and weak evidence that anyone read the notes. With AI-drafted documentation, that gap gets wider, so make review before signing a written expectation.


## What an unsigned note costs in an audit


In a Medicare ADR, a missing signature triggers a process before a denial. The reviewer offers the 20-day attestation window. If the signature was required and the attestation doesn't resolve it, the claim can be denied. If missing or illegible signatures raise doubts about whether the record is genuine, the reviewer should consider a UPIC referral. During TPE, the PIM treats a missing signature as an easy error you can cure with an attestation mid-probe.


Prepayment review and Medicaid are less forgiving. As our guide to[prepayment review in behavioral health](https://blog.adentris.com/prepayment-review-behavioral-health/) explains, every claim is scored, and CareSource's prepayment policy denies claims whose records lack a valid provider signature. A state rule that requires a signed note, like Minnesota's statute or Montana's Medicaid manual, leaves an unsigned note short of what the claim needs. In a statistical sample, each of those claims becomes an error that can be projected across your billing.


Finding the problem yourself creates its own clock. If an internal review shows paid Medicare claims backed by notes that can't be fixed, that can be an identified overpayment, which generally must be reported and returned within 60 days (42 CFR 401.305). For the audit programs that pull these records, see our overview of[Medicare and Medicaid audits in behavioral health](https://blog.adentris.com/medicare-medicaid-audits-behavioral-health/) .


## An unsigned-note aging control


Signature problems are mostly timing problems, so manage them like aging AR. Here's the control I'd set up, calibrated to a three-business-day rule. Shift the days to match your strictest requirement.


Note age What happens Owner


Day 0, end of day Daily unsigned-note report sent to each clinician, plus a co-signature queue to each supervisor EHR report or compliance


Day 1 Reminder to the clinician. Claim stays on hold until the note is signed Clinician, billing


Day 2 Escalation to the clinical supervisor, who clears the note or the co-signature that day Supervisor


Day 3, the deadline Clinical director notified. Compliance logs the note as late Clinical director, compliance


Past the deadline Completed only as a labeled late entry. Compliance decides whether the service can be billed Compliance


Monthly Late and unsigned rates by clinician and program, reviewed in supervision Compliance, clinical leadership


Two rules make the table work. Billing never releases a claim on an unsigned note. And nobody signs, attests or co-signs for someone else, whatever the backlog looks like.

## Frequently asked questions


**What are Medicare's signature requirements for medical records?**


The person responsible for the care must be identifiable, through a handwritten or electronic signature, and the record must show the date of service. Illegible signatures can be supported with a signature log or attestation. Stamped signatures aren't accepted unless the author has a physical disability and can prove it. The rules are in Medicare Program Integrity Manual, Chapter 3, §3.3.2.4.


**How long does a clinician have to sign a progress note?**


Medicare sets no fixed number of days, but expects documentation at the time of service. States and payers often do set one. California requires most Medi-Cal behavioral health progress notes within three business days, Minnesota requires SUD treatment services to be documented within seven days, and some commercial policies require signatures before the claim is submitted.


**What is a signature attestation statement?**


It is a signed and dated statement in which the author of a record entry confirms that the entry and signature are theirs. Medicare accepts attestations for most missing or illegible signatures, regardless of when they were created, but not for orders that require a signature, not from anyone other than the author, and never to backdate a document that had to be signed by a set date.


**Can a clinician add a late entry or late signature to a note?**


Yes, if the late entry is labeled as such, shows the real date and author, and leaves the original entry intact. CMS expects amendments, corrections and delayed entries to be clearly and permanently marked. Dating a new entry to look as if it was written on the day of service is backdating, which reviewers treat as falsification.


**Is a signature log required?**


No, but it helps whenever initials or signatures are hard to read. Medicare reviewers must consider a signature log regardless of when it was created and can't deny a claim because the log lacks credentials. A log identifies a signature that exists. It doesn't replace a missing one.


**Do pre-licensed clinicians' notes need a supervisor co-signature?**


It depends on the payer and state. Minnesota requires treatment supervisor approval of trainees' assessments and treatment plans within 10 business days, and California Medi-Cal counts co-signatures toward its three-business-day deadline. Medicare bills incident-to services under the supervising practitioner, and some commercial plans don't accept pre-licensed clinicians as rendering providers at all.
